Run a standing program (many units, many patches, few owner turns) from the main session: you decide which worker does each piece and check what each produces; you do not write the code. One task driven to a predicate is `autonomous-run`; work one worker can finish inside its budget is not a program.

1. Plan the units in a plan file (`.omp/plans/<name>.md`) and keep the program state there and in `skill://decision-log`. Each unit has one goal, exact paths it may and may not touch, and the evidence that proves it done (a command and its expected output, or an artifact). A unit whose evidence you cannot name is not scoped yet.
2. Topology: one coordinator level. The main session is the only coordinator (recursion depth 1): it plans units, spawns every worker directly and fans them out in waves. No sub-coordinators, and no worker spawns anything. Cap about ten workers in flight; start the next as each finishes. Workers see only their brief, so a brief carries each upstream result it depends on as a path, not pasted text. Watch workers with the blocking wait only: no scripts, no polling loops, and no relaying messages or status between agents.
3. Brief limits: `agent/RULES.md` "Worker briefs". A worker that returns partial results after a compaction stop is replaced by smaller new workers, not re-sent the same brief.
4. Run one unit end to end as a canary (brief, worker, read the patch, apply, run the check) before fanning out, so a flaw in the brief costs one worker. Near-identical cheap units: the first unit is that test.
5. Per patch: read the patch against the brief, `git apply` it (`git apply --check` first when patches touch the same files), and run the unit's check yourself. Look first for removed assertions in test files (a `-` line holding `expect`, `assert`, or a test declaration); a removed or loosened assertion needs the reason in the brief, otherwise send the patch back. A worker that edited a shared tree directly or returned only status text has not delivered. Green CI or a worker's summary is an input to a verdict, not the verdict; a verdict covers one head.
6. Judge workers by side effects (patch files, changed paths, check output), not status text. Never message a worker to check on it: a message restarts an idle worker, and the side effects tell you. A worker that stalls or loops is stopped and replaced. Retry by cause: a smaller scope after a context limit, the same brief after a dropped run, a changed approach after a tool error or a failed check. After two retries drop the unit, log the cause, and replan around it. A late result is checked against the current tree, and its unique findings go to a new worker.
7. Send back work that drifts from scope or grows past what was asked; keep only fixes that block the program and park the rest as units. Each PR gets a verifier that did not author it, on a different tier where possible, and nothing merges without that verifier's pass at the current head; under `autopilot-full` only the main session merges. Review for risky patches goes to a worker that did not author the change (`reviewer`; `security-reviewer` for security; `deep-reviewer` only for one-way doors). Workers never push, open or merge PRs, deploy or write to GitHub: they return patches, and you run every external action, checking live state with `gh` first.
8. A worker whose request count does not move across two checks may be dead while still listed as running: read the last line of its session file (`history://<id>`, or `~/.omp/agent/sessions/<project>/<session>/<id>.jsonl`). `stopReason: "error"` (a 429 rate limit, a provider error) means it is gone: cancel it and respawn the same brief once the limit clears, instead of waiting on it.
9. Account for every worker you spawned as done, replaced, or absorbed into another worker's scope, then run the program's predicate once on the merged tree. Ask the owner only for an irreversible action, a product or preference call no experiment settles, or a dead end that survived a replan.

Reply: in Korean, plain text: what landed against the goal, each unit's verdict with its evidence, what was dropped and why, and the decisions waiting on the owner.
